## Aid as a Windfall

Your government receives $500 million from abroad: no goods produced, arrives every year.

. . .

Think of it like oil revenue or winning the lottery at the country level.

. . .

::: incremental
- Does it foster development?
- Does it crowd out domestic effort?
- Does it change who the government is accountable to?
:::

## If Used Well

::: incremental
- **Savings gap**: external capital breaks the low-income → low-savings → low-investment cycle
- **Public goods**: courts, roads, power grids; markets won't build them
- **Big push**: some investments only pay off if many happen at once; aid can coordinate
:::

## Even If Used Well

::: incremental
- **Dutch disease**: large inflows appreciate the currency, making exports expensive and contracting manufacturing
- **Accountability shift**: a government funded by donors answers to donors, not citizens
:::

## If Used Poorly

::: incremental
- **Fungibility**: aid frees up domestic funds already earmarked for the same thing. Reinikka & Svensson (2004): 13 cents per dollar reached Ugandan schools
- **Corruption**: aid passes through many hands; weak institutions mean diversion at every step
- **Misallocation**: Briggs (2016): multilateral aid within countries flows to middle-income regions, not the poorest
:::

## Empirical Evidence

::: incremental
- **Burnside & Dollar (2000)**: positive, but only with good policy
- **Rajan & Subramanian (2008)**: no robust effect, even with good policy
- **Hansen & Tarp (2001)**: positive but diminishing returns
- Micro-level RCTs: often positive for specific, well-targeted programs
:::

. . .

The macro evidence is mixed. Is this real heterogeneity, or a measurement problem?

# Clemens, Radelet, Bhavnani & Bazzi (2012)

## Four Decades, Three Answers

::: incremental
- **Boone (1996)**: no effect on investment or growth across 96 countries
- **Burnside & Dollar (2000)**: aid raises growth, but only with good policy
- **Rajan & Subramanian (2008)**: no robust effect, even with good policy
- Similar data. Similar periods. Three different conclusions
:::

## Two Fixable Problems

::: incremental
- CRBB argue the divergence comes from two resolvable research design choices
- **Measurement**: what counts as aid, and over what time horizon?
- **Identification**: how do you separate the effect of aid from the effect of everything that moves with aid?
:::

## Time Horizon

::: incremental
- A road raises productivity for decades. Food relief addresses a crisis this week
- Testing whether **all aid** raises GDP **this year** is asking whether food relief builds roads
- The time horizon should depend on what type of aid you are measuring
:::

## Aid Types

::: incremental
- **Early-impact**: budget support, roads, energy, agriculture. Plausible growth effect within a few years
- **Long-horizon**: education, health, technical cooperation. Growth effects arrive over a generation
- **No growth mechanism**: humanitarian aid, food relief, emergency assistance
:::

. . .

Early-impact aid is roughly 45 to 53% of total flows.

## Decision 1: Lag

Data is in 4-year periods; aid arrives in period $t$.

::: incremental
- **(a) Same period**: current growth affects how much aid countries receive. Reverse causation
- **(b) Next period**: allows time for aid to work. Severs the contemporaneous feedback loop
- **(c) 10 years later**: plausible for infrastructure, but most of the sample disappears
:::

. . .

CRBB choose **(b)**: does Aid($t-1$) predict Growth($t$)?

## Decision 2: Aid

Your data includes roads, food relief, vaccination campaigns, budget support, technical cooperation.

::: incremental
- **(a) All disbursements**: most flows have no short-run growth mechanism. Testing noise
- **(b) Project aid only**: misses budget support, which can fund productive investment
- **(c) Early-impact only**: aid that could plausibly raise productive capacity in a few years
:::

. . .

CRBB choose **(c)**. About 45 to 53% of total flows.

## The Causal Problem

Even with the right measure and the right lag, a problem remains.

::: incremental
- Countries that receive more aid tend to be poorer and slower-growing
- Aid and low growth travel together in the data
- Is aid **causing** slow growth, or is slow growth **causing** more aid?
:::

## The Causal Challenge

```{r dag-aid, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=3.8, fig.align='center'}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 0.8, y = 2.2, xend = 3.2, yend = 2.2,
           linewidth = 1.1, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.22, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 2.42, size = 3,
           label = "via investment, imports, public goods") +
  annotate("segment", x = 2, y = 3.6, xend = 0.4, yend = 2.55,
           linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "dashed",
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "open")) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2, y = 3.6, xend = 3.6, yend = 2.55,
           linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "dashed",
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "open")) +
  annotate("segment", x = 3.3, y = 1.9, xend = 0.7, yend = 1.9,
           linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "dashed",
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "open")) +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 1.63, size = 2.7, color = "gray40",
           label = "reverse causation: poorer or slower-growing countries attract more aid") +

  annotate("label", x = 2, y = 3.82, label = "Unobserved confounders (U_i)",
           size = 3.2, fontface = "italic", label.padding = unit(0.35, "lines"),
           label.r = unit(0.15, "lines"), fill = "gray95", color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = 0.88, size = 2.9, color = "gray40",

  theme_void()
```

## Decision 3: Confounders

Poor, conflict-prone countries attract more aid and grow more slowly.

::: incremental
- **(a) Add country controls**: you cannot observe everything
- **(b) First-difference**: subtract each country's own past values. Geography, institutions, colonial history cancel out
- **(c) Find an instrument**: prior studies used population size, but population affects growth directly through trade and market size. The instrument fails
:::

. . .

CRBB choose **(b)**.

## FE vs. First-Differencing

::: incremental
- **Country FE**: deviation from country long-run mean. Was Nigeria above its own average when aid was higher?
$$y_{it} - \bar{y}_i = \beta(\text{Aid}_{i,t-1} - \overline{\text{Aid}}_i)$$
- **First-difference**: change from previous period. Did Nigeria grow faster when aid increased?
$$\Delta y_{it} = \beta \,\Delta\text{Aid}_{i,t-1}$$
- FD is stricter: it removes slow-moving country trends, not just the fixed mean
:::

## What They Find

::: incremental
- Results consistent across all three reanalyzed datasets
- **+1 pp in Aid/GDP** is followed on average by:
  - **+0.1 to 0.2 pp** in annual real GDP per capita growth
  - **+0.3 to 0.5 pp** in Investment/GDP
- Positive but modest. Strong diminishing returns: effect turns negative at high aid levels
:::

## Is This Actually Causal?

Lagging breaks the contemporaneous feedback, but two threats remain:

::: incremental
- **Donor foresight**: donors anticipate growth and front-load aid; but CRBB show they systematically mis-forecast recipient growth
- **Mean reversion**: bad growth attracts aid AND predicts recovery. See next slide
:::

## Mean Reversion

```{r mean-reversion, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.height=4.2, fig.align='center'}
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
n <- 200
parent_h <- rnorm(n, 175, 9)
child_h  <- 0.5 * parent_h + 87.5 + rnorm(n, 0, 6)

ggplot(data.frame(p = parent_h, c = child_h), aes(p, c)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, color = "#011F5B", size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#990000", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray55", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 158, y = 194, label = "slope = 1\n(no reversion)", size = 3, color = "gray45") +
  annotate("text", x = 192, y = 174, label = "actual slope\n(regression to mean)", size = 3, color = "#990000") +
  labs(x = "Parent height (cm)", y = "Child height (cm)",
       title = "Galton (1886): very tall parents have tall children, but not as tall as themselves") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

## Aid and Mean Reversion

The same logic applies to country growth rates.

::: incremental
- A country has a terrible growth year. Donors respond with more aid
- The next period, growth recovers, partly because bad years do not persist
- A researcher observes: aid was followed by growth
- But the recovery may have happened regardless
:::

## Design Choices

Three studies, similar data, three different answers: the divergence came from measurement and identification choices.

::: incremental
- **What you measure**: aggregate aid vs. early-impact aid
- **When you measure**: contemporaneous vs. lagged
- **How you identify**: name the source of clean variation and defend why it is not driven by outcomes
:::

. . .

Every design choice either makes a null result informative or stacks the deck against finding one.

## What the Paper Argues

::: incremental
- Fix the design choices and three datasets give the same answer
- Aid causes some growth on average: modest, with wide variation across recipients
- High aid dependence shows diminishing returns. It cannot substitute for domestic investment
- "Aid does not work" was a methodological artifact replicated across three influential papers
:::

# Why This Matters Now

## US Aid Has Collapsed

```{=html}
<!-- Replace with chart: US ODA 2000-2025, e.g. OECD DAC or devex.com screenshot -->
```

::: incremental
- The US is historically the world's largest bilateral donor
- In early 2025, the Trump administration dismantled USAID and froze most foreign assistance
- Dozens of countries lost their primary external funding source within weeks
:::

## Who Gets Hurt?

::: incremental
- Countries where aid is 10 to 20% of GDP face acute fiscal shortfalls with no capacity to absorb them
- Sub-Saharan Africa: highest aid dependence, weakest domestic revenue base
- Health programs (HIV treatment, malaria, TB) face immediate disruption
- Aid cuts reduce investment and remove shock buffers in the countries least able to absorb them
:::
